precentral gyrus.kid: This is the part of your brain that gives the orders, telling the muscles all over your body when to move.
precentral gyrus.d: Lies in the frontal lobe just anterior to the central sulcus and is the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4), organised as a motor homunculus of the contralateral body. Middle cerebral artery infarction mostly causes contralateral face and upper-limb weakness, whereas anterior cerebral artery infarction mainly causes lower-limb weakness.

prostate.kid: A small chestnut-shaped gland under a boy's bladder that makes a fluid to protect sperm.
prostate.d: Lies below the bladder neck, surrounding the prostatic urethra, with the rectum immediately posterior. Benign hyperplasia causes voiding difficulty; stress urinary incontinence is common after prostatectomy and is a key indication for pelvic floor muscle training.

proximal phalanx of big toe.kid: The bone of your big toe closest to the sole of your foot, which works the hardest when you push off to walk.
proximal phalanx of big toe.d: The base articulates with the head of the first metatarsal to form the first metatarsophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the distal phalanx to form the interphalangeal joint. The base gives attachment to flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, adductor hallucis and extensor hallucis brevis; hallux valgus and hallux rigidus both occur at the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

proximal phalanx of fourth toe.kid: The little bone of your fourth toe closest to the sole of your foot, which helps the toe bend and grip the ground.
proximal phalanx of fourth toe.d: The base articulates with the head of the fourth metatarsal to form the metatarsophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The fourth dorsal interosseous attaches to the lateral side of the base and the second plantar interosseous to the medial side.

proximal phalanx of index finger.kid: The bone of your pointer finger closest to your palm, which lets the finger bend and point at things.
proximal phalanx of index finger.d: The base articulates with the head of the second metacarpal to form the metacarpophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The first dorsal interosseous attaches to the radial side of the base and the first palmar interosseous to the ulnar side; the flexor tendon sheath and A2 pulley lie on its palmar surface.

proximal phalanx of little finger.kid: The bone of your pinky finger closest to your palm, which helps your hand squeeze tight when you hold things.
proximal phalanx of little finger.d: The base articulates with the head of the fifth metacarpal to form the metacarpophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis attach to the ulnar side of the base, and the third palmar interosseous attaches to the radial side.

proximal phalanx of little toe.kid: The little bone of your pinky toe closest to the sole of your foot, which helps the outer edge of your foot stand steady.
proximal phalanx of little toe.d: The base articulates with the head of the fifth metatarsal to form the metatarsophalangeal joint. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis attach to the lateral side of the base and the third plantar interosseous to the medial side; phalangeal fractures from stubbing the toe on furniture are common here.

proximal phalanx of middle finger.kid: The bone of your middle finger closest to your palm, and the longest of all the finger bones.
proximal phalanx of middle finger.d: The base articulates with the head of the third metacarpal to form the metacarpophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The second and third dorsal interossei attach to either side of the base; the middle finger is the axis for abduction and adduction of the hand.

proximal phalanx of ring finger.kid: The bone of your ring finger closest to your palm, which helps the finger bend and hold on to things.
proximal phalanx of ring finger.d: The base articulates with the head of the fourth metacarpal to form the metacarpophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The fourth dorsal interosseous attaches to the ulnar side of the base and the second palmar interosseous to the radial side.

proximal phalanx of second toe.kid: The little bone of your second toe closest to the sole of your foot, which helps hold your body up when you walk.
proximal phalanx of second toe.d: The base articulates with the head of the second metatarsal to form the metatarsophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The first and second dorsal interossei attach to either side of the base, the second toe being the axis for abduction and adduction of the foot; hammer toe is common in this toe.

proximal phalanx of third toe.kid: The little bone of your third toe closest to the sole of your foot, which helps the toe bend and grip the ground.
proximal phalanx of third toe.d: The base articulates with the head of the third metatarsal to form the metatarsophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the middle phalanx to form the proximal interphalangeal joint. The third dorsal interosseous attaches to the lateral side of the base and the first plantar interosseous to the medial side.

proximal phalanx of thumb.kid: The bone of your thumb closest to your palm, which lets the thumb bend so you can pinch things.
proximal phalanx of thumb.d: The base articulates with the head of the first metacarpal to form the metacarpophalangeal joint, and the head articulates with the distal phalanx to form the interphalangeal joint (the thumb has only two phalanges). The base gives attachment to flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis, adductor pollicis and extensor pollicis brevis; injury to the ulnar collateral ligament of the metacarpophalangeal joint is skier's thumb.

pulmonary artery.kid: The big blood tube that carries used blood, which has run out of oxygen, from your heart to your lungs to pick up fresh oxygen.
pulmonary artery.d: The pulmonary trunk divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; they are among the few arteries that carry deoxygenated blood. A dislodged deep vein thrombus after prolonged bed rest or surgery can cause pulmonary embolism, so watch for sudden dyspnoea and chest pain.

pulmonary valve.kid: A little door at the exit of the heart's lower right room that lets blood flow only toward the lungs and never back again.
pulmonary valve.d: Lies between the right ventricular outflow tract and the pulmonary trunk and consists of three semilunar cusps. It is auscultated at the second intercostal space at the left sternal border; its closure produces the P2 component of the second heart sound.

pulmonary vein.kid: The blood tubes that carry fresh blood, filled up with oxygen in the lungs, back to your heart.
pulmonary vein.d: There are two on each side (superior and inferior pulmonary veins), four in total draining into the left atrium; they are among the few veins that carry oxygenated blood. The region around the pulmonary vein ostia is a common origin of the abnormal electrical discharges of atrial fibrillation.

putamen.kid: A clump of nerve cells deep inside your brain that helps your movements stay smooth and not shaky.
putamen.d: Together with the caudate nucleus it forms the striatum, and together with the globus pallidus the lentiform nucleus; it is the main input station of the basal ganglia motor circuit. Dopamine depletion in Parkinson's disease is most marked here, and it is also the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.

radius.kid: The long bone on the thumb side of your forearm, which lets you turn your palm up and down.
radius.d: Landmarks: head, radial tuberosity (biceps brachii insertion), styloid process, dorsal tubercle (Lister's tubercle) and ulnar notch. It takes part in the humeroradial joint, the proximal and distal radioulnar joints and the radiocarpal joint; a fall on an outstretched hand commonly causes a distal radius fracture (Colles fracture).

rectum.kid: The last part of your large intestine, where poop waits until you go to the toilet.
rectum.d: Extends from about the third sacral vertebra to the anal canal, lying anterior to the sacrum and coccyx; puborectalis forms the anorectal angle that maintains continence. Defecation dysfunction is associated with poor pelvic floor muscle coordination and is a focus of assessment in pelvic floor physical therapy.

renal artery.kid: The blood tube that carries blood into your kidney so the kidney can filter the waste out of it.
renal artery.d: Arises from each side of the abdominal aorta at about the level of L1-L2; the right renal artery is longer and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava. Renal blood flow is about one fifth of cardiac output; renal artery stenosis can cause secondary hypertension.

renal vein.kid: The blood tube that carries the blood your kidney has cleaned back toward your heart.
renal vein.d: Lies anterior to the renal artery and drains into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer, passing anterior to the abdominal aorta between it and the superior mesenteric artery (compression here is nutcracker syndrome), and receives the left gonadal and suprarenal veins.

sacrum.kid: The big upside-down triangle bone at the very bottom of your spine, which passes the weight of your upper body on to your hips.
sacrum.d: Formed by fusion of five sacral vertebrae. Landmarks: sacral promontory, ala, auricular surface, anterior and posterior sacral foramina, median sacral crest and sacral hiatus. It articulates above with L5 at the lumbosacral joint, laterally with the ilia at the sacroiliac joints, and below with the coccyx.

scaphoid.kid: A boat-shaped bone on the thumb side of your wrist, and the one most likely to break when you fall and catch yourself with your hand.
scaphoid.d: The most lateral bone of the proximal carpal row, with the scaphoid tubercle and waist as landmarks; it is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox. It articulates with the radius, lunate, capitate, trapezium and trapezoid; its blood supply runs retrograde from the distal end, so the proximal pole is prone to avascular necrosis or nonunion after fracture.

scapula.kid: The flat triangle bone on your back that looks like a wing and lets your arm lift high and move in every direction.
scapula.d: Landmarks: spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, subscapular fossa, superior and inferior angles, and medial border. It takes part in the glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints and forms the functional scapulothoracic joint with the thorax; scapulohumeral rhythm and scapular winging are key points of assessment.

second costal cartilage.kid: The bendy cartilage that joins your second rib to your breastbone, so your chest can spring in and out when you breathe.
second costal cartilage.d: Attaches on either side of the sternal angle (the junction of the manubrium and body of the sternum), making it an important palpation starting point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces. The second sternocostal joint is a synovial joint divided by an intra-articular ligament; it is one of the common sites of costochondritis.

second lumbar vertebra.kid: The second bone of your lower back, big and thick, which helps hold up the weight of your upper body.
second lumbar vertebra.d: The body is broad and the spinous process is quadrangular and projects horizontally backward; the superior and inferior facet joint surfaces lie close to the sagittal plane, favouring flexion and extension while limiting rotation. In adults the conus medullaris ends at about the L1-L2 level, with the cauda equina below; the left crus of the diaphragm and psoas major attach here.

second metacarpal bone.kid: The long bone in your palm that connects to your pointer finger, and the steadiest bone in your palm.
second metacarpal bone.d: The base articulates mainly with the trapezoid and also contacts the trapezium, capitate and third metacarpal; its carpometacarpal joint has very little mobility, making it a stable pillar of the hand. Extensor carpi radialis longus inserts on the dorsal base and flexor carpi radialis on the palmar base; the head forms the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger.

second metatarsal bone.kid: The long bone in your foot that connects to your second toe, and the longest of the long bones in your foot.
second metatarsal bone.d: The base is wedged between the medial and lateral cuneiforms and articulates with the intermediate cuneiform, making it the keystone of Lisfranc joint stability with the least mobility. It lies on the longitudinal axis of the foot and is the most common site of march fracture (stress fracture).

second rib.kid: The second rib at the top of your chest, which works with the other ribs to protect your heart and lungs.
second rib.d: Its costal cartilage attaches at the sternal angle, a surface landmark for counting ribs. The lateral surface bears the tuberosity for serratus anterior and gives attachment to scalenus posterior; the head articulates with the bodies of T1 and T2 at the costovertebral joint, and the tubercle with the transverse process of T2 at the costotransverse joint.

second thoracic vertebra.kid: The second bone of your upper back, with the second pair of ribs attached on each side.
second thoracic vertebra.d: Each side of the body bears superior and inferior costal facets and the transverse process bears a transverse costal facet, articulating with the rib head and rib tubercle respectively; the spinous process is long and slopes downward. Hypomobility of the upper thoracic spine is often associated with neck and shoulder pain, and this is a segment commonly treated in manual therapy.

seminal vesicle.kid: A pair of little pouches behind a boy's bladder that make a fluid to feed sperm.
seminal vesicle.d: Lies posterior to the base of the bladder and anterior to the rectum, secreting a fructose-rich fluid that makes up about 60-70% of semen volume. Its duct joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra.

septal papillary muscle of ventricle.kid: A tiny muscle inside your heart that pulls on a valve with thin little strings so blood cannot flow backward.
septal papillary muscle of ventricle.d: Lies on the septal wall of the right ventricle; it is small and often multiple, and is connected by chordae tendineae to the septal and anterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve. During ventricular contraction the papillary muscles tighten the chordae, preventing the leaflets from everting into the right atrium.

septum pellucidum.kid: A thin sheet right in the middle of your brain that separates the left and right rooms filled with brain water.
septum pellucidum.d: A thin double-layered membrane stretched between the corpus callosum and the fornix, separating the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles. It is a landmark for judging the midline on imaging; like the adjacent septal nuclei, it is a structure related to the limbic system.

sesamoid bone of foot.kid: Little bean-like bones under the base of your big toe that protect the tendon and help you push when you walk.
sesamoid bone of foot.d: The medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) sesamoids are embedded in the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis, lying on the plantar aspect of the first metatarsal head and articulating with it; they increase the flexor moment arm and bear forefoot load. Sesamoiditis and stress fractures are common in people who run, jump or dance.

set of anterior cardiac veins.kid: A few small blood tubes on the front of your heart that bring the blood the heart muscle has used back into the heart.
set of anterior cardiac veins.d: They collect venous blood from the anterior wall of the right ventricle, cross the coronary sulcus and drain directly into the right atrium, without returning through the coronary sinus.

set of eyebrows.kid: The two rows of hair above your eyes that stop sweat and rain from running into your eyes.
set of eyebrows.d: Lie over the supraorbital margin and are moved by frontalis, corrugator supercilii and orbicularis oculi. Raising the eyebrows tests the temporal branch of the facial nerve; in peripheral facial palsy the affected side cannot raise the eyebrow and the forehead wrinkles disappear, whereas in central palsy frontalis function is preserved.

set of head hairs.kid: The hair that grows on top of your head, keeping it warm, blocking the sun and protecting your scalp.
set of head hairs.d: Grows from the scalp, with follicles lying in the dermis to subcutaneous layer; it provides insulation, sun protection and cushioning. Of the five layers of the scalp, the galea aponeurotica connects frontalis and occipitalis and is relevant to palpation assessment of tension-type headache.

set of interventricular septal branches.kid: Small blood tubes that dig into the wall in the middle of your heart to bring food to the heart muscle inside that wall.
set of interventricular septal branches.d: Septal branches from the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery supply the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum, and septal branches from the posterior interventricular branch of the right coronary artery supply the posterior third. The septum contains the atrioventricular bundle and the left and right bundle branches, so ischaemia can cause conduction block.

set of nasal cartilages.kid: The soft, bendy pieces that hold up the shape of your nose, which is why you can wiggle the tip of your nose around.
set of nasal cartilages.d: Comprise the septal cartilage, lateral nasal cartilages, major alar cartilages and minor alar cartilages, forming the framework of the lower half of the external nose and keeping the nasal valve patent. Septal deviation or traumatic deformity increases nasal resistance and affects the nasal breathing pattern.

set of posterior veins of ventricle.kid: Small blood tubes on the back of your heart that gather the blood the heart muscle has used and send it back.
set of posterior veins of ventricle.d: Refers to the posterior vein of the left ventricle, which ascends along the diaphragmatic surface (posteroinferior wall) of the left ventricle, collects venous blood from the myocardium there, and drains into the coronary sinus or the great cardiac vein.

set of pubic hairs.kid: The hair that grows on the lower tummy when you grow up, which protects the skin and cuts down on rubbing.
set of pubic hairs.d: Distributed over the mons pubis in front of the pubic symphysis and around the external genitalia; it grows at puberty under the influence of sex hormones and is a secondary sexual characteristic. The underlying pubic symphysis and pubic tubercle are landmarks for pelvic palpation.

seventh cervical vertebra.kid: This is the bone that sticks out the most at the back of your neck when you look down.
seventh cervical vertebra.d: The spinous process is long and not bifid, making it the most obvious palpation landmark at the cervicothoracic junction (vertebra prominens). Its transverse foramen is small and the vertebral artery usually does not pass through it; it forms the cervicothoracic junction with T1 below, gives attachment to the ligamentum nuchae, and occasionally bears a cervical rib that causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

seventh costal cartilage.kid: The cartilage that joins your seventh rib to your breastbone, and the last one to connect straight to the breastbone.
seventh costal cartilage.d: The last pair of costal cartilages to attach directly to the sternum, joining at the junction of the lower end of the sternal body and the xiphoid process; it forms interchondral joints with the sixth and eighth costal cartilages and makes up the upper part of the costal margin. Rectus abdominis and the diaphragm attach to it.

seventh rib.kid: The seventh rib in your chest, and the last rib that connects straight to your breastbone.
seventh rib.d: The last pair of true ribs and a typical rib, with a head, neck, tubercle, angle and costal groove. The head articulates with the bodies of T6 and T7 and the tubercle with the transverse process of T7; the lower ribs increase the transverse diameter of the thorax by bucket-handle movement.

seventh thoracic vertebra.kid: The seventh bone in the middle of your back, at about the height of the bottom edge of your shoulder blades.
seventh thoracic vertebra.d: A typical thoracic vertebra whose long spinous process slopes markedly downward and overlaps the vertebra below. In standing, the inferior angle of the scapula corresponds approximately to the level of the T7 spinous process, a landmark for palpation; its costal facets on each side articulate with the seventh and eighth ribs.

sixth cervical vertebra.kid: The sixth bone of your neck, which protects the spinal cord inside and lets your neck turn.
sixth cervical vertebra.d: The anterior tubercle of its transverse process is especially prominent and is called the carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle), against which the common carotid artery can be compressed. The vertebral artery usually enters the transverse foramen at this level; on the surface it corresponds approximately to the cricoid cartilage, and C5-C6 is a common segment for disc degeneration.

sixth costal cartilage.kid: The cartilage that joins your sixth rib to your breastbone, letting your rib cage open up when you breathe.
sixth costal cartilage.d: Connects the sixth rib to the lower part of the sternal body and forms an interchondral joint (a synovial joint) with the seventh costal cartilage. Pectoralis major and rectus abdominis attach to it, and the costal cartilages provide the elastic recoil the thorax needs for breathing.

sixth rib.kid: The sixth rib in your chest, which protects your heart and lungs like a bar of a cage.
sixth rib.d: A typical true rib with a head, neck, tubercle, angle and costal groove (containing the intercostal vessels and nerve). The head articulates with the bodies of T5 and T6 and the tubercle with the transverse process of T6; it is one of the attachment sites of serratus anterior and external oblique.

sixth thoracic vertebra.kid: The sixth bone in the middle of your back, with ribs attached on each side to protect your chest.
sixth thoracic vertebra.d: A typical thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, superior and inferior costal facets, transverse costal facets, and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. The facet joint surfaces lie close to the coronal plane, favouring rotation and side bending; the mid-thoracic spine is where the apex of the thoracic kyphosis lies.

skin.kid: The coat that wraps your whole body, keeping germs out and water in, and letting you feel hot, cold and pain.
skin.d: The largest organ of the body, made up of the epidermis, the dermis and the underlying subcutaneous tissue, with barrier, thermoregulatory, sensory and vitamin D synthesis functions. Clinical priorities include dermatomal sensory testing, pressure injury prevention, scar and wound care, and oedema assessment.

sphenoid bone.kid: A butterfly-shaped bone hidden right in the middle of your skull that holds up the bottom of your brain.
sphenoid bone.d: Landmarks: body and sella turcica (housing the pituitary gland), greater wing, lesser wing, medial and lateral pterygoid plates, optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. The lateral pterygoid plate is the origin of the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles and so is relevant to temporomandibular joint function; the bone articulates with almost all the other cranial bones.

spleen.kid: An organ in the upper left of your tummy that filters your blood, clears out old red blood cells and helps fight germs.
spleen.d: Lies in the left upper abdomen deep to ribs 9-11 and is the largest lymphoid organ, responsible for blood filtration and immune responses. Fractures of the left lower ribs are readily complicated by splenic rupture; contact sports should be suspended when infectious mononucleosis causes splenomegaly.

splenic artery.kid: The blood tube that carries blood to your spleen, winding its way along the pancreas.
splenic artery.d: The largest branch of the coeliac trunk, running a tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the pancreas to the splenic hilum. Along the way it gives off pancreatic branches, the short gastric arteries and the left gastro-omental artery, supplying the body and tail of the pancreas and the fundus of the stomach.

splenic vein.kid: The blood tube that carries blood away from your spleen and sends it on to your liver.
splenic vein.d: Runs posterior to the pancreas, receives the inferior mesenteric vein, and then joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. Portal hypertension can cause splenomegaly.

stem of coronary artery.kid: The very first stretch of the blood tube that branches off the body's biggest artery just to bring blood to the heart muscle.
stem of coronary artery.d: Refers to the left main coronary artery, which arises from the left aortic sinus, runs between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle, and promptly divides into the anterior interventricular branch (left anterior descending) and the circumflex branch, supplying most of the left ventricle. Occlusion of the main stem causes extensive myocardial infarction with a grave prognosis.

stomach.kid: A bag-like organ in your tummy that churns up the food you eat and turns it into mush.
stomach.d: Lies in the left upper abdomen and is divided into the cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part; it carries out initial digestion with gastric acid and peristalsis and is innervated by the vagus nerve. For patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux, exercise and positioning should avoid lying flat after meals and excessive increases in intra-abdominal pressure.

stria medullaris of thalamus.kid: A small bundle of nerve fibres on top of a part of your brain called the thalamus, carrying messages through the brain like a wire.
stria medullaris of thalamus.d: A fibre bundle running along the dorsomedial border of the thalamus, carrying information from the septal nuclei, hypothalamus and other areas to the habenular nuclei of the epithalamus. It is a connecting pathway of the limbic system and is involved in the regulation of emotion and motivation.

stria terminalis.kid: A thin bundle of nerve fibres in your brain that helps carry messages to do with feelings.
stria terminalis.d: The main efferent fibre bundle of the amygdala, running in the groove between the caudate nucleus and the thalamus and terminating in the hypothalamus and septal area. It is involved in regulating stress, anxiety, and autonomic and endocrine responses.

subclavian artery.kid: A big blood tube that runs under your collarbone, carrying blood to your arm, neck and brain.
subclavian artery.d: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and from the aortic arch on the left, passes between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, and becomes the axillary artery after crossing the outer border of the first rib. Its branches are the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery, thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk and dorsal scapular artery; it is one of the structures compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome.

subclavian vein.kid: A big blood tube that runs under your collarbone, bringing blood from your arm back to your heart.
subclavian vein.d: The continuation of the axillary vein, running anterior to scalenus anterior between the clavicle and the first rib and joining the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein, with the lymphatic ducts draining into the junction. It is a common site for central venous catheter placement; repetitive overhead activity can cause effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome).

superior colliculus.kid: A little bump on the back of your brainstem that lets your eyes and head turn quickly toward what you see.
superior colliculus.d: Lies in the tectum on the dorsal aspect of the midbrain, integrating visual, auditory and somatosensory information and controlling saccadic eye movements and head-eye orienting reflexes. It influences the neck muscles through the tectospinal tract and is relevant to vestibular and oculomotor rehabilitation.

superior frontal gyrus.kid: The topmost fold at the front of your brain, which helps you plan movements and concentrate on your thinking.
superior frontal gyrus.d: Lies in the upper part of the frontal lobe above the superior frontal sulcus; the medial surface of its posterior part contains the supplementary motor area, which takes part in motor planning, sequencing and bilateral coordinated movement, while the anterior part is involved in executive functions such as working memory. Damage to the supplementary motor area can cause difficulty initiating movement.

superior mesenteric artery.kid: A big blood tube in your tummy that carries blood to your small intestine and part of your large intestine.
superior mesenteric artery.d: Arises from the anterior wall of the abdominal aorta at about the level of L1 and descends posterior to the neck of the pancreas and anterior to the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supplies the midgut derivatives, from the distal duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon; occlusion causes acute intestinal ischaemia.

superior mesenteric vein.kid: The blood tube that carries the goodness your small intestine soaks up from food along with the blood to your liver.
superior mesenteric vein.d: Runs to the right of the superior mesenteric artery, collecting venous blood from the small intestine, caecum, ascending colon and transverse colon. It joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein, delivering absorbed nutrients to the liver.

superior parietal lobule precuneus.kid: An area toward the back of the top of your brain that helps you know where your body is and where things are.
superior parietal lobule precuneus.d: The superior parietal lobule lies on the upper lateral surface of the parietal lobe and the precuneus is its continuation on the medial surface (Brodmann areas 5 and 7); together they form the somatosensory association cortex, integrating proprioceptive and visuospatial information to guide limb movement. Damage can cause astereognosis, optic ataxia and contralateral neglect.

superior vena cava.kid: The big blood tube that gathers all the used blood from your head, neck and arms and sends it back to your heart.
superior vena cava.d: Formed by the union of the left and right brachiocephalic veins behind the right first costal cartilage; it receives the azygos vein and enters the right atrium at about the level of the third costal cartilage. Compression by a mediastinal tumour can cause superior vena cava syndrome, with swelling of the head, neck and upper limbs.

supramarginal gyrus.kid: A fold on the side of your brain that helps you understand speech and also helps you do well-practised movements.
supramarginal gyrus.d: Lies in the inferior parietal lobule, curving around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus (Brodmann area 40), and takes part in phonological processing and the integration of skilled movement. Damage in the dominant hemisphere can cause conduction aphasia and ideomotor apraxia, while damage on the non-dominant side is associated with spatial neglect.

talus.kid: The bone inside your ankle that passes the weight of your lower leg on to your foot and lets your foot move up and down.
talus.d: Landmarks: head, neck, body and trochlea (wider anteriorly and narrower posteriorly, so the ankle joint is most stable in dorsiflexion). It articulates above with the tibia and fibula at the talocrural joint, below with the calcaneus at the subtalar joint, and anteriorly with the navicular; it has no muscle attachments, and fractures of the neck are prone to avascular necrosis.

temporal bone.kid: The bone on each side of your head next to your ear, which protects the inner parts of the ear that look after hearing and balance.
temporal bone.d: Landmarks: mastoid process (sternocleidomastoid insertion), styloid process, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa and articular tubercle, external acoustic meatus, and petrous part (containing the inner ear and vestibular organs). The mandibular fossa and the condylar process of the mandible form the temporomandibular joint, making this bone relevant to temporomandibular disorders and vestibular rehabilitation.

tenth rib.kid: The tenth rib low down in your chest, whose front end is joined by cartilage to the rib above it.
tenth rib.d: A false rib whose costal cartilage merges upward into the ninth costal cartilage, forming the lower border of the costal margin. The head usually has only a single articular facet, articulating with the body of T10; the diaphragm and abdominal muscles attach to it, and laxity of the costal cartilage can cause slipping rib syndrome.

tenth thoracic vertebra.kid: The tenth bone of your spine, sitting just above your lower back, with the tenth pair of ribs attached on each side.
tenth thoracic vertebra.d: Each side of the body has only one complete costal facet, articulating with the head of the tenth rib, and the transverse costal facet is small or absent. Because the lower ribs splint the thorax less, the lower thoracic spine has more flexion-extension mobility than the upper thoracic spine; on the surface it corresponds approximately to the level of the xiphoid process.

testis.kid: A pair of little balls in a boy's scrotum that make sperm and male hormones once he grows up.
testis.d: Lies within the scrotum, producing sperm and secreting testosterone; it is suspended by the spermatic cord, with the cremaster muscle regulating its position and temperature. Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain during exercise must raise suspicion of testicular torsion and warrants immediate referral to the emergency department.

thalamus.kid: A relay station right in the centre of your brain that passes the feeling messages from your body on to all the different parts of the brain.
thalamus.d: The largest nuclear mass of the diencephalon and the relay station for all sensory input ascending to the cortex except olfaction (ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei), while the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei relay motor information from the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Thalamic stroke can cause contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.

third cervical vertebra.kid: The third bone of your neck, which holds up the weight of your head and lets your neck bend and turn.
third cervical vertebra.d: A typical cervical vertebra with uncinate processes, a short bifid spinous process and transverse foramina (transmitting the vertebral artery); its facet joint surfaces are inclined at about 45 degrees. On the surface it corresponds approximately to the level of the hyoid bone; dysfunction of the C2-C3 facet joint is a common source of cervicogenic headache.

third costal cartilage.kid: The cartilage that joins your third rib to your breastbone, letting your chest move when you breathe.
third costal cartilage.d: Connects the third rib to the body of the sternum, forming a synovial sternocostal joint. The sternocostal part of pectoralis major attaches to its surface; like the second costal cartilage, it is a common site of costochondritis and Tietze syndrome.

third lumbar vertebra.kid: The bone right in the middle of your lower back, very big and thick, which holds up the weight of your body.
third lumbar vertebra.d: Lies at the apex of the lumbar lordosis and has the longest transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, giving attachment to quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia; excessive traction can cause L3 transverse process syndrome. The facet joint surfaces lie close to the sagittal plane, favouring flexion and extension; on the surface it corresponds to a level slightly above the umbilicus.

third metacarpal bone.kid: The long bone right in the middle of your palm that connects to your middle finger, and the central pillar of your palm.
third metacarpal bone.d: The base articulates with the capitate and bears a styloid process on its dorsolateral aspect, where extensor carpi radialis brevis inserts; its carpometacarpal joint is stable, making it the central column of the longitudinal arch of the hand. The transverse head of adductor pollicis arises from its palmar surface, and the head forms the metacarpophalangeal joint of the middle finger.

third metatarsal bone.kid: The long bone in the middle of your foot that connects to your third toe and helps hold up your weight when you walk.
third metatarsal bone.d: The base forms a tarsometatarsal joint with the lateral cuneiform and also meets the bases of the second and fourth metatarsals, while the head forms the third metatarsophalangeal joint. Like the second metatarsal, it is a common site of stress fracture; the space between the third and fourth metatarsal heads is the most common location of Morton's neuroma.

third rib.kid: The third rib in the upper part of your chest, which joins the other ribs in wrapping around your heart and lungs.
third rib.d: A typical true rib with a head, neck, tubercle, angle and costal groove. The head articulates with the bodies of T2 and T3 and the tubercle with the transverse process of T3; pectoralis minor and serratus anterior attach to it, and the upper ribs increase the anteroposterior diameter of the thorax by pump-handle movement.

third thoracic vertebra.kid: The third bone of your upper back, at about the height of the bony ridge across the top of your shoulder blade.
third thoracic vertebra.d: A typical thoracic vertebra with superior and inferior costal facets, transverse costal facets and a downward-sloping spinous process. In standing, the medial end of the spine of the scapula corresponds approximately to the level of the T3 spinous process, a landmark for palpation; the rhomboids and trapezius attach to the spinous process.

third ventricle.kid: A narrow little room right in the middle of your brain, filled with the fluid that protects your brain.
third ventricle.d: A narrow midline cavity between the thalami and hypothalamus of the two sides, communicating with the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina and with the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct. Obstruction of the aqueduct causes obstructive hydrocephalus, enlarging the lateral and third ventricles.

thyroid cartilage.kid: The hard cartilage you can feel at the front of your neck, which guards the vocal cords that make your voice, like a shield.
thyroid cartilage.d: The largest cartilage of the larynx; its two laminae meet anteriorly to form the laryngeal prominence, at about the level of C4-C5, a landmark for neck palpation. The inferior horn forms the cricothyroid joint with the cricoid cartilage to adjust vocal fold tension; sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor attach to it.

tibia.kid: The big, thick, hard bone at the front of your lower leg, which holds up the weight of your whole body.
tibia.d: Landmarks: medial and lateral condyles and tibial plateau, intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament insertion), Gerdy's tubercle (iliotibial tract insertion), anterior border, soleal line and medial malleolus. It takes part in the knee joint, the proximal and distal tibiofibular joints and the ankle joint; medial tibial stress syndrome and stress fractures are common.

trachea.kid: The tube that runs from your throat to your lungs, which is the path the air you breathe in takes to get there.
trachea.d: Extends from the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (about C6) to the level of the sternal angle (about T4-T5), where it divides into the left and right main bronchi; it is supported by 16-20 C-shaped cartilage rings, with the trachealis muscle forming the posterior wall. Mucociliary clearance and the cough mechanism are the basis of airway clearance techniques.

trapezium.kid: A small wrist bone at the base of your thumb that lets your thumb swivel around freely.
trapezium.d: The most lateral bone of the distal carpal row, with the tubercle of the trapezium and a groove for the flexor carpi radialis tendon on its palmar surface. It forms the saddle-shaped carpometacarpal joint of the thumb with the first metacarpal (a common site of osteoarthritis) and also articulates with the scaphoid, trapezoid and second metacarpal.

trapezoid.kid: A tiny bone in your wrist that firmly holds the palm bone below your pointer finger.
trapezoid.d: The smallest bone of the distal carpal row, wedge-shaped. It articulates distally with the base of the second metacarpal, proximally with the scaphoid, laterally with the trapezium and medially with the capitate; it is stably positioned and is very rarely fractured in isolation.

tricuspid valve.kid: The door between the upper and lower rooms on the right side of your heart, with three flaps that stop blood from flowing backward.
tricuspid valve.d: The atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, made up of anterior, posterior and septal leaflets connected by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles. It is auscultated at the fourth to fifth intercostal space at the left border of the lower sternum; its closure contributes to the first heart sound.

triquetral.kid: A small bone on the pinky side of your wrist, shaped like a three-sided pyramid.
triquetral.d: Lies on the ulnar side of the proximal carpal row, with an oval facet on its palmar surface for the pisiform; it articulates laterally with the lunate and distally with the hamate, and proximally faces the ulna across the triangular fibrocartilage complex. It is the second most commonly fractured carpal bone, mostly as dorsal avulsion fractures.

trunk of coronary artery.kid: The main blood tube that wraps around the outside of your heart, bringing oxygen and food to the heart muscle.
trunk of coronary artery.d: Refers to the main trunk of the right coronary artery, which arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus around to the diaphragmatic surface of the heart. It supplies the right atrium, the right ventricle and, in most people, the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes; occlusion causes inferior wall myocardial infarction, often with bradycardia or atrioventricular block.

tuber cinereum.kid: A little bump at the bottom of your brain that is joined to the pituitary gland, the boss of your hormones.
tuber cinereum.d: A grey matter eminence on the floor of the hypothalamus between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies, extending downward as the infundibulum to connect with the pituitary gland. Its median eminence is where hypothalamic releasing hormones enter the hypophyseal portal system, regulating endocrine function.

twelfth rib.kid: The lowest and shortest rib, whose front end is not joined to anything, so it is called a floating rib.
twelfth rib.d: A floating rib, short and lacking a neck, tubercle and angle; its head has a single articular facet that articulates only with the body of T12. Quadratus lumborum, the diaphragm and the thoracolumbar fascia attach to it, and deep to it lie the upper part of the kidney and the costodiaphragmatic recess.

twelfth thoracic vertebra.kid: The last bone of the chest part of your spine, which joins the lower back bones below and holds the shortest ribs.
twelfth thoracic vertebra.d: The thoracolumbar transitional vertebra: its superior articular processes are thoracic in type (near the coronal plane) and its inferior articular processes lumbar in type (near the sagittal plane); each side of the body has a single costal facet and the transverse processes have none. Stress concentrates at the thoracolumbar junction, making this one of the most common segments for compression fracture.

ulna.kid: The long bone on the pinky side of your forearm; the pointy bump at the back of your elbow is part of it.
ulna.d: Landmarks: olecranon (triceps brachii insertion), coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity (brachialis insertion), and the head and styloid process. It takes part in the humeroulnar joint and the proximal and distal radioulnar joints; distally it is separated from the carpal bones by the triangular fibrocartilage complex and does not take part directly in the radiocarpal joint.

upper central secondary incisor tooth.kid: The big front tooth right in the middle of your top row, which cuts food like a little shovel.
upper central secondary incisor tooth.d: The largest maxillary incisor, single-rooted, erupting at about 7-8 years; it cuts food and assists with speech and anterior guidance of the occlusion. It is innervated by the anterior superior alveolar nerve and is the tooth most often injured by impact in sport or falls.

upper first secondary molar tooth.kid: A big tooth at the back of your top row that comes in at about age six and grinds your food up.
upper first secondary molar tooth.d: Erupts at about 6 years and is commonly called the six-year molar; it usually has three roots (two buccal and one palatal), with the root apices close to the floor of the maxillary sinus. It is the reference tooth for classifying occlusal relationships (Angle classification), and its occlusal position affects loading of the temporomandibular joint.

upper first secondary premolar tooth.kid: The tooth behind the pointy tooth in your top row, with two little points that help crush food.
upper first secondary premolar tooth.d: Has two cusps, buccal and palatal, and in most cases two roots (buccal and palatal); it erupts at about 10-11 years, replacing a primary molar. It is innervated by the middle superior alveolar nerve and is a tooth commonly extracted for orthodontic treatment.

upper lateral secondary incisor tooth.kid: The smaller front tooth next to your big front tooth, which helps bite food off.
upper lateral secondary incisor tooth.d: Lies distal to the central incisor and is similar in form but smaller, single-rooted, erupting at about 8-9 years. It is innervated by the anterior superior alveolar nerve and is a tooth position where morphological variation (such as a peg-shaped tooth) and congenital absence are relatively common.

upper lobe of lung.kid: The very top part of your lung, which fills with air when you breathe in and hands the oxygen over to your blood.
upper lobe of lung.d: The right upper lobe is separated from the middle and lower lobes by the horizontal and oblique fissures, and the left upper lobe is separated from the lower lobe by the oblique fissure and includes the lingula; the apex of the lung projects above the medial third of the clavicle. Postural drainage positions and auscultation sites for the upper lobe segments (apical, posterior and anterior) are key points in chest physical therapy.

upper second secondary molar tooth.kid: A big tooth even further back in your top row that comes in at about age twelve and is used for grinding food.
upper second secondary molar tooth.d: Erupts at about 12 years and is commonly called the twelve-year molar; it usually has three roots that lie closer together than those of the first molar, with the root apices close to the maxillary sinus. It is innervated by the posterior superior alveolar nerve and shares the main masticatory load with the first molar.

upper second secondary premolar tooth.kid: The tooth in front of the big back teeth in your top row, which helps crush food before passing it back to be ground up.
upper second secondary premolar tooth.d: Has two cusps of similar size, buccal and palatal, and usually a single root, erupting at about 10-12 years. It is innervated by the middle superior alveolar nerve, and its root apex lies close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.

upper secondary canine tooth.kid: The pointy fang in your top row, the longest tooth in your mouth, used for tearing food.
upper secondary canine tooth.d: Has a single cusp and the longest root in the mouth, lies at the corner of the dental arch, and erupts at about 11-12 years. During lateral excursion of the mandible it provides canine guidance, separating the posterior teeth to protect the temporomandibular joint and the posterior teeth; it is a tooth position prone to impaction.

ureter.kid: A long, thin tube that joins your kidney to your bladder and carries the pee your kidney makes down to the bladder.
ureter.d: About 25 cm long and retroperitoneal, it descends along the anterior surface of psoas major, crosses the iliac vessels, enters the pelvis and drains into the bladder. It has three physiological constrictions (the ureteropelvic junction, the crossing of the iliac vessels and the intramural part within the bladder wall); an impacted stone produces colicky pain radiating from the loin to the groin, which must be differentiated from low back pain.

urethra.kid: The little tube your pee flows through from your bladder to the outside of your body.
urethra.d: About 4 cm long in females and about 20 cm in males, where it is divided into prostatic, membranous and spongy parts. The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle innervated by the pudendal nerve; together with the pelvic floor muscles it maintains urinary continence and is a target of pelvic floor muscle training for urinary incontinence.

urinary bladder.kid: A balloon-like bag low down in your tummy that stores your pee and makes you want to go when it is full.
urinary bladder.d: Lies posterior to the pubic symphysis; the detrusor muscle contracts under the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4 parasympathetic), whereas sympathetic innervation promotes urine storage. After spinal cord injury a reflexic or areflexic neurogenic bladder can occur depending on the level of the lesion, a key focus of rehabilitation and pelvic floor therapy.

vomer.kid: A thin sheet of bone inside your nose that divides the inside of your nose into a left side and a right side.
vomer.d: A single thin plate of bone forming the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum. Superiorly it meets the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the body of the sphenoid, inferiorly the nasal crests of the maxilla and palatine bone, and its anterior border meets the septal cartilage; the posterior border is free and separates the two choanae.

wall of heart.kid: The wall of your heart, made mostly of very strong muscle that squeezes and relaxes to pump blood all around your body.
wall of heart.d: From inside out it consists of the endocardium, myocardium and epicardium (visceral pericardium); the myocardium is supplied by the coronary arteries, and the left ventricular wall is the thickest. After myocardial infarction the ejection fraction is affected according to the extent of damage, which is the basis for setting exercise prescription intensity in cardiac rehabilitation.

white matter structure of cerebral hemis.kid: The white part inside your brain, like lots of wires that link all the different parts of the brain together.
white matter structure of cerebral hemis.d: Made up of myelinated nerve fibres, classified as association fibres, commissural fibres (such as the corpus callosum) and projection fibres (corona radiata and internal capsule). The corticospinal tract passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so even a small lacunar infarct can cause contralateral hemiplegia; multiple sclerosis also affects the white matter.

xiphoid process.kid: The little pointed tip at the very bottom of the breastbone in the middle of your chest, which is soft cartilage when you are little.
xiphoid process.d: The lowest part of the sternum, forming the xiphisternal joint with the sternal body at about the level of T9-T10 and gradually ossifying in adulthood. Rectus abdominis, the linea alba and the diaphragm attach to it; it should be avoided during chest compressions so that it does not fracture and injure the liver.

zygomatic bone.kid: The bone that sticks out on your cheek, which gives your cheek its shape and also protects the outer side of your eye.
zygomatic bone.d: Forms the prominence of the cheek and the lateral wall and floor of the orbit. Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch, the origin of masseter; it also meets the frontal bone via its frontal process and articulates with the maxilla and the greater wing of the sphenoid, and gives attachment to zygomaticus major and minor.
